lessons.title: 1. Hiragana, katakana and kanji
lessons.subtitle: The three writing systems · Where each is used · Romaji

explanations.title: Three kinds of characters
explanations.body: Japanese is written with three kinds of characters: hiragana, katakana and kanji. All three can appear in one sentence. Hiragana and katakana, like an alphabet, stand for sounds. Kanji, or Chinese characters, stand for meanings as well as sounds.

examples.text: テレビを 見ます。
examples.translation: Terebi o mimasu. — I watch television.

explanations.title: What each one is used for
explanations.body: In 「テレビを 見ます」, テレビ is katakana, 見 is kanji, and を and ます are hiragana.

rows: Verb and adjective endings, function words such as particles, and native Japanese words not covered by kanji
Nouns and the stems of verbs and adjectives; they carry meaning

explanations.title: Rōmaji
explanations.body: There is a fourth system, rōmaji (Roman letters). It is used for station names, signs and so on. In this course rōmaji appears under the Japanese as a help; do not lean on it, because the aim is to read the real characters. The romaji here follows the Genki books: a long vowel is written double (sensee, ookii), and the particles は, へ and を are spelled by sound (wa, e, o).

explanations.title: The small っ
explanations.body: Another small letter, っ, is used to write double consonants such as tt, kk, pp and ss. The consonant that follows っ is held for one extra beat, so the sound of a pause appears in the word. A short pause changes the word: かった (katta, won) and かた (kata, shoulder) are different words.

explanations.title: A double n
explanations.body: A double n, as in さんねん (sannen, three years), is written with ん plus a kana that begins with an n sound (な, に, ぬ, ね or の). The ん counts as its own beat.

explanations.title: Long vowels
explanations.body: When the same vowel is written twice in a row, the vowel is pronounced about twice as long as a single one. Hold it long enough, because the length changes the word.

explanations.title: The long ee and oo
explanations.body: The long ee is usually written by adding い to an e-column kana (せいかつ). In a few words, え is used instead (えいが is written with い, but おねえさん uses え). The long oo is in most cases written by adding う to an o-column kana, but a few words use お for historical reasons.

explanations.title: Words that differ by vowel length
The sound of ん
explanations.body: ん has the length of a full syllable, but its sound depends on what follows it. Japanese speakers are not normally aware of the differences, so you need not worry about them. Before n, t, d, s and z it is “n”, as in おんな (onna, woman). Before m, p and b it is “m”, as in さんぽ (sampo, stroll). Before k and g it is “ng” as in “song”, as in まんが (manga, comics). Before a vowel or at the end of a word it nasalizes the vowel before it, as in ほん (book) and れんあい (romance).

explanations.title: Vowels that are dropped
explanations.body: The vowels i and u are sometimes dropped when they stand between voiceless consonants (k, s, t, p and h), or at the end of an utterance after one. For example, すきです sounds like “s(u)kides(u)”.

examples.text: すきです。
examples.translation: Suki desu. — (I) like it.

explanations.title: Accent
explanations.body: Japanese has pitch accent. Every syllable is pronounced at about the same length and stress, and is either high or low in pitch. English stress accent, by contrast, makes syllables longer and louder. Pitch patterns vary a lot by region. This course does not mark accent; do not worry about it, and imitate the audio you hear. For example: あさ (morning), なまえ (name) and たかい (high; expensive) are pronounced with different pitch patterns.

explanations.title: Choose the correct hiragana
explanations.body: The book’s Practice A: pick the right kana of a look-alike pair for the romaji. The answers: yo よ (not ま), ho ほ (not は), me め (not ぬ), su す (not む), ki き (not さ), chi ち (not さ), ta た (not に), ro ろ (not る), e え (not ん). Look-alike pairs are the heart of learning kana: ぬ/め, は/ほ, さ/き/ち, る/ろ, ま/よ.

lessons.title: 12. Kanji: what they are and how they work
lessons.subtitle: 音読み と 訓読み · Four kinds of kanji · Joyo kanji

explanations.title: What kanji are
explanations.body: Kanji are Chinese characters, introduced to Japan more than 1,500 years ago, when the Japanese language did not yet have a writing system. Hiragana and katakana developed later in Japan from simplified Chinese characters. Kanji represent both meanings and sounds.

explanations.title: Two kinds of readings
explanations.body: Most kanji have more than one reading. There are two kinds: on-yomi (Chinese readings) come from the pronunciation used in China at the time; some kanji have several on-yomi because of changes over time and across regions. Kun-yomi (Japanese readings) were added when people began to use kanji to write native Japanese words.

explanations.title: How many kanji
explanations.body: By the time of high school graduation, Japanese are expected to know 2,136 kanji, called the Joyo kanji, which the Ministry of Education designates as commonly used. 1,006 are taught at the elementary school level, and most of the rest in junior high school.

explanations.title: Four kinds of kanji by how they are formed
explanations.body: Roughly four types, by formation:

rows: dots and lines for numbers or abstract ideas
日 (sun) + 月 (moon) → 明 (bright); 人 (person) + 木 (tree) → 休 (to rest)
a meaning element and a sound element
氵 (water) + 青 (sei) → 清 (sei, clean); 日 (sun) + 青 (sei) → 晴 (sei, clear sky)

explanations.title: おはよう, ありがとう: short and long forms
explanations.body: おはよう is used between friends and family members, while おはよう ございます is used between less intimate acquaintances; the same goes for ありがとう and ありがとう ございます. The rule of thumb: if you are on a first-name basis with someone, go for the shorter versions. If you would address someone as Mr. or Ms., use the longer versions.

explanations.title: おはよう is for the morning
explanations.body: おはよう is the greeting used before noon, but some people use it in casual settings in the afternoon, or even at night, when they see their classmates or co-workers for the first time that day.

explanations.title: さようなら
explanations.body: There are several good-bye expressions in Japanese, and the choice depends on the degree of separation. さようなら indicates that the speaker does not expect to see the person spoken to before she “turns a page in her life”: not until a new day arrives, or until fate brings the two together again. It sounds dramatic and ritualistic, and its daily use is largely restricted to school children taking leave of their teachers.

rows: See you.; See you later. (between friends)

explanations.title: すみません: three meanings
explanations.body: すみません means (1) “Excuse me,” to get another person’s attention, (2) “I’m sorry,” to apologize for the trouble you have caused, or (3) “Thank you,” to show appreciation for what someone has done for you.

explanations.title: いいえ
explanations.body: いいえ is primarily “No,” a negative reply to a question. In the dialogue it is used to express the English phrase “Don’t mention it” or “You’re welcome,” with which you point out that one is not required to feel obliged for what you have done for them.

explanations.title: いってきます, いってらっしゃい, ただいま, おかえりなさい
explanations.body: いってきます and いってらっしゃい are a common exchange used at home when a family member leaves. The person who leaves says いってきます, literally “I will go and come back.” The family members answer いってらっしゃい, “Please go and come back.” ただいま and おかえり are used when a person comes home. The person who arrives says ただいま (“I am home right now”) to the family members, and they respond with おかえりなさい (“Welcome home”).

explanations.title: Culture note: greetings and bowing
explanations.body:
Japanese people greet each other by bowing, which has many other functions, such as expressing respect, gratitude, or apologies. There are different ways of bowing, ranging from a small nod of the head to a 45-degree bend at the waist. Generally, the longer and the deeper you bow, the more formal and respectful it appears to others.

Many Japanese tend to feel uncomfortable with physical contact, although handshaking is becoming quite common in business situations, especially those involving foreigners.

When meeting someone in a business situation for the first time, it is customary to exchange meishi (business cards) with a small bow. Etiquette guides list a vast number of rules and pointers, but just remember that the important thing is to clearly show your respect when exchanging meishi.

explanations.title: Numbers
explanations.body: Numbers from zero to one hundred. Above ten, the tens and the ones are put side by side: じゅう (10) + いち (1) = じゅういち (11); に (2) + じゅう (10) = にじゅう (20); にじゅうさん is 23.

explanations.title: Other readings
explanations.body: Some numbers have a second reading. 0 is ゼロ or れい. 4 is usually よん, but し and よ appear in some combinations (よじ, four o’clock; よねんせい, fourth-year student). 7 is なな, but しち in しちじ (seven o’clock). 9 is きゅう, but く in くじ (nine o’clock).

rows: じゅうなな、じゅうしち
じゅうきゅう、じゅうく

explanations.title: Expression Note: numbers with changing sounds
explanations.body: Many number words have more than one pronunciation. For example: 1 is いち, but いっ in いっぷん (one minute) and いっさい (one year old). 2 is に, but when reading digits one by one (as in a phone number) it may be pronounced with a long vowel, にい. 3 is さん; the part after it may change shape, as in さんぷん, not さんふん. 4 is よん, but よねんせい and よじ; in some later combinations it is し (しがつ, April), and the part after it may change, as in よんぷん. 5 is ご; read out separately, it may be pronounced ごう. 6 is ろく, but ろっ in ろっぷん. 7 is なな, but しちじ for seven o’clock. 8 is はち, but usually はっ in はっぷん and はっさい. 9 is きゅう, but くじ for nine o’clock. 10 is じゅう, but じゅっ or じっ in じゅっぷん/じっぷん and じゅっさい/じっさい.

explanations.title: Time: hours
explanations.body: Add じ to the number. ごぜん (A.M.) and ごご (P.M.) go in front of the hour, and はん (half) goes after it.

examples.text: いま ごぜん くじです。
examples.translation: Ima gozen kuji desu. — It is nine in the morning now.

examples.text: いま ごご さんじはんです。
examples.translation: Ima gogo sanji han desu. — It is half past three in the afternoon now.

explanations.title: Time: minutes
explanations.body: Minutes use ふん or ぷん after the number, with some sound changes. The numbers 1, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 10 take ぷん (with small っ for 1, 6, 8 and 10); the others take ふん. For minutes 11–19 and for 20 and 30, the same endings follow the tens.

rows: じゅうはっぷん、じゅうはちふん
にじゅっぷん、にじっぷん
さんじゅっぷん、さんじっぷん

explanations.title: Age
explanations.body: Add さい after the number for “…years old.” The question is なんさい (How old are you?); おいくつ is a more polite way to ask. 20 years old is はたち, though にじゅっさい or にじっさい can also be used.

lessons.title: 20. Grammar 1: X は Y です and questions with か
lessons.subtitle: わたしは がくせいです · りゅうがくせいですか · なん, なんじ, なんさい, なんねんせい

explanations.title: です: “It is …”
explanations.body: “It is 12:30.” “I am a student.” “My major is the Japanese language.” All of these are expressed with a noun and the word です. Note that none of these sentences has a “subject” like the “it,” “I” and “my major” of the English versions. Sentences without subjects are very common in Japanese; speakers tend to omit the subject whenever they think it is clear to the listener what or who they are referring to.

examples.text: じゅうにじはんです。
examples.translation: Juuniji han desu. — (It) is half past twelve.

examples.text: がくせいです。
examples.translation: Gakusee desu. — (I) am a student.

examples.text: にほんごです。
examples.translation: Nihongo desu. — (My major) is the Japanese language.

explanations.title: XはYです
explanations.body: When it is not clear what is being talked about, we can say X は …, where X stands for the thing that is talked about, the “topic.” The pattern X は Y です identifies a person or a thing X as item Y: “X is Y. As for X, it is Y.” は is a particle: it attaches to a phrase and shows how it relates to the rest of the sentence. It is written は but pronounced wa.

examples.text: せんこうは にほんごです。
examples.translation: Senkoo wa nihongo desu. — (My) major is the Japanese language.

examples.text: わたしは スー・キムです。
examples.translation: Watashi wa Suu Kimu desu. — I am Sue Kim.

examples.text: やましたさんは せんせいです。
examples.translation: Yamashita-san wa sensee desu. — Mr. Yamashita is a teacher.

examples.text: メアリーさんは アメリカじんです。
examples.translation: Mearii-san wa amerikajin desu. — Mary is an American.

explanations.title: No “a” and no plural
explanations.body: Nouns like がくせい and せんせい stand alone, unlike the English “student” and “teacher,” which are preceded by “a.” Japanese has no item that corresponds to “a,” nor to the plural “-s.” Without background, a sentence like がくせいです is ambiguous: it may mean “We are / you are / they are students” as well as “I am / you are / she is a student.”

explanations.title: Questions: add か
explanations.body: It is very easy to form questions in Japanese: add か at the end of a statement. It is not customary to write a question mark at the end of a question sentence in Japanese. This is a “yes/no” question:

examples.text: りゅうがくせいです。
examples.translation: Ryuugakusee desu. — (I am) an international student.

examples.text: りゅうがくせいですか。
examples.translation: Ryuugakusee desu ka. — (Are you) an international student?

explanations.title: Question words
explanations.body: Question sentences can contain a question word like なん (what). In this lesson you learn: なんじ (what time), なんさい (how old), なんねんせい (what year in school). The question word for “what” has two pronunciations: なん is used immediately before です or before a counter like じ (o’clock); なに is used before a particle, and also in the word なにじん (person of what nationality).

examples.text: せんこうは なんですか。
examples.translation: Senkoo wa nan desu ka. — What is your major?

examples.text: せんこうは えいごです。
examples.translation: Senkoo wa eego desu. — (My major) is English.

examples.text: いま なんじですか。
examples.translation: Ima nanji desu ka. — What time is it now?

examples.text: いま くじです。
examples.translation: Ima kuji desu. — It is nine o’clock.

examples.text: メアリーさんは なんさいですか。
examples.translation: Mearii-san wa nansai desu ka. — How old are you, Mary?

examples.text: じゅうきゅうさいです。
examples.translation: Juukyuusai desu. — I’m nineteen years old.

examples.text: なんねんせいですか。
examples.translation: Nannensee desu ka. — What year are you in college?

examples.text: にほんじんですか。

lessons.title: 21. Grammar 2: noun の noun, names, and expression notes
lessons.subtitle: たけしさんの でんわばんごう · だいがくの せんせい · にほんの だいがく · あの · はい / ええ · さん

explanations.title: noun の noun
explanations.body: の is a particle that connects two nouns. The phrase さくらだいがくの がくせい means “a student at Sakura University.” The second noun, がくせい, provides the main idea (being a student), and the first, さくらだいがく, makes it more specific (not a high school but a college student). の is very versatile: in the first example below it acts like the English possessive (’s), but that is not the only role it can play.

examples.text: たけしさんの でんわばんごう
examples.translation: Takeshi-san no denwa bangoo — Takeshi’s phone number

examples.text: だいがくの せんせい
examples.translation: Daigaku no sensee — a college professor

examples.text: にほんごの がくせい
examples.translation: Nihongo no gakusee — a student of the Japanese language

examples.text: にほんの だいがく
examples.translation: Nihon no daigaku — a college in Japan

explanations.title: Word order: main idea last
explanations.body: In the first two examples the English and Japanese words are arranged in the same order; in the last two they are in the opposite order. Japanese is more consistent: the main idea always comes at the end, with any further description placed before it. A phrase of the form “noun の noun” acts more or less like one big noun. You can put it wherever you can put a noun:

examples.text: たけしさんの おかあさんは こうこうの せんせいです。
examples.translation: Takeshi-san no okaasan wa kookoo no sensee desu. — Takeshi’s mother is a high school teacher.

explanations.title: Culture note: Japanese names
explanations.body: When Japanese give their name, they say their family name first and their given name last (middle names do not exist). When introducing themselves they often say only their family name. Most Japanese names are written in kanji. For example, たなか is usually written 田中, which means “middle of the rice field.” Family names are often related to nature or geographical features. Because many kanji share the same reading, names with the same pronunciation may be written with different kanji; ゆうこ can be written 優子 or with other characters.

explanations.title: あの
explanations.body: あの indicates that you have some reservations about saying what you are going to say next. You may be worried about interrupting something someone is currently doing, or about sounding rude by asking personal questions, for example.

examples.text: あの、りゅうがくせいですか。
examples.translation: Ano, ryuugakusee desu ka. — Um… are you an international student?

explanations.title: はい / ええ
explanations.body: Both はい and ええ mean “yes” in response to yes-no questions. Compared to はい, ええ is more conversational and relaxed. In more informal situations, うん is used. はい is also used to respond to a knock at the door or to the calling of one’s name, meaning “Here.” (ええ cannot be used in that case.)

examples.text: はい。
examples.translation: Hai. — Yes. / Here.

examples.text: ええ、そうです。
examples.translation: Ee, soo desu. — Yes, that’s right.

explanations.title: そうですか
explanations.body: そうですか acknowledges that you have understood what was just said: “Is that so?” or “I see.”

examples.text: そうですか。
examples.translation: Soo desu ka. — I see.

explanations.title: Pronunciation of は
explanations.body: The particle は is pronounced “wa,” not “ha.” It should be written with は. All other instances of “wa” are written with わ. There are a few exceptions, such as こんにちは (good afternoon) and こんばんは (good evening), which are usually written with は.

examples.text: わたしの でんわばんごうは さん なな の はち ろく ろく ななです。
examples.translation: Watashi no denwa bangoo wa san nana no hachi roku roku nana desu. — My telephone number is 37-8667.

explanations.title: Giving your telephone number
explanations.body: The particle の is usually placed between the local exchange code and the last four digits. So 012-345-6789 is ゼロ いち に、さん よん ご の ろく なな はち きゅう.

explanations.title: せんせい
explanations.body: The word せんせい is usually reserved for describing somebody else’s occupation. わたしは せんせいです makes sense, but may sound slightly arrogant, because せんせい actually means an “honorable master.” If you (or a member of your family) are a teacher and want to be really modest, you can use the word きょうし instead.

examples.text: きょうし
examples.translation: Kyooshi — teacher (modest)

explanations.title: さん
explanations.body: さん is placed after a name as a generic title. It goes both with a given name and a family name. Children are referred to as ちゃん (and boys in particular as くん) rather than さん. Professors and doctors are usually referred to with the title せんせい. さん and other title words are never used in reference to oneself.

explanations.title: Referring to the person you are talking to
explanations.body: The word for “you,” あなた, is not very commonly used in Japanese. Instead, we use the name and a title like さん and せんせい to refer to the person we are talking to. So “Ms. Hart, are you Swedish?” should be the first sentence below, not the second.
